result.excerpt: it is now possible look back at how China decided to respond to Trump's tariff pressure.
result.claim: How did China respond to Trump's tariff pressure in phase one of the trade war, and what does that imply for the deal and future US strategy?
result.reason: A negotiated pause is the right moment to infer a rival's strategy from its revealed behavior.

result.excerpt: Five points stand out to me…
result.claim: China's response comes down to five lessons: no concessions on industrial policy, currency buffering without reserve loss, no use of Treasuries as a weapon, little targeting of US manufactures, and heavy targeting of agriculture and energy.
result.reason: An adversary's revealed choices under pressure show which levers it values and which it lacks.

result.excerpt: China never was prepared—it seems from the outside—to negotiate on China 2025 or the subsidies and procurement preferences at the center of its industrial policies.
result.claim: China refused to negotiate on its core industrial policies, namely the subsidies and procurement preferences of China 2025.
result.reason: States do not trade away policies they see as central to future growth.

result.excerpt: China's determination to preserve an import-substituting industrial strategy almost guarantees future trade conflict.
result.claim: Import substitution aimed at technological independence will cut China's imports of advanced manufactures and lead partners to question keeping their markets open, which makes future conflict close to certain.
result.reason: Market access tends to be reciprocal, so a country that stops importing invites closure of its export markets.

result.excerpt: But these trends won't play out over the next year—Boeing has bigger problems right now than the C919
result.claim: The effects of import substitution are long-run and will not significantly affect China's 2020 imports.
result.reason: Structural industrial shifts take years to show up in trade flows.

result.excerpt: The yuan has fallen by 8 percent vs. the dollar and 4 percent vs. a broad basket since May 2018.
result.claim: The yuan fell 8% against the dollar and 4% against a broad basket, which helped China's overall exports hold up while its exports to the US fell.
result.reason: A weaker currency offsets tariff costs and supports exports to other markets.

result.excerpt: In part, that is because China tightened its controls on outflows back in late 2016 and early 2017, and those controls worked.
result.claim: The depreciation did not trigger 2015-style panic because of tighter capital controls, fewer bank carry trades, the yuan's appeal as a reserve alternative to negative-yielding euros, moves sized to the tariffs, and a rising trade surplus.
result.reason: Currency moves cause capital flight only when outflows are possible and the move signals further declines.

result.excerpt: But I don't think many expected that China would be able to keep its reserves stable through the trade war
result.claim: Contrary to common expectations, China managed the yuan while keeping its reserves stable.
result.reason: Managing a depreciating currency is usually expected to require reserve sales.

result.excerpt: the two standard indicators of Chinese intervention suggest either no activity over the course of 2019 (the PBOC's balance sheet) or small purchases (the settlement data).
result.claim: In 2019 the PBOC balance sheet shows no intervention, the settlement data show small purchases, and the balance of payments shows a tiny reserve sale.
result.reason: Multiple intervention proxies should be compared because each captures different flows.

result.excerpt: even now Chinese data never quite fully lines up, which bothers me more than most
result.claim: Chinese official data never fully reconcile, which reduces confidence in the reserve measures.
result.reason: Statistics that fail to reconcile internally warrant skepticism.

result.excerpt: China's Treasury holdings are down just a bit, but only a bit after you take into account China's not so hidden holdings in Belgian custodial accounts.
result.claim: China did not dump Treasuries: holdings fell only slightly once Belgian custodial accounts are counted, and the shifts reflected a search for yield in Agencies and currency-hedged yen bonds.
result.reason: Reserve holdings must be traced through custodians to measure true ownership.

result.excerpt: in an era where central banks have recognized that balance sheet expansion (see this paper from my friend Ramin Toloui) and yield curve control are part of the monetary policy toolkit
result.claim: The author takes as given that modern central banks will use balance sheet expansion and yield curve control to cap yields.
result.reason: Central banks now treat asset purchases as a normal instrument for steering long-term rates.

result.excerpt: China presumably realized it didn't actually have much leverage here—if it tried to push Treasury yields up, the Fed would react.
result.claim: Selling Treasuries gives China little leverage because the Fed can offset any rise in yields, and the alternative assets yield less.
result.reason: A central bank willing to buy its own bonds neutralizes a foreign holder's threat to sell.

result.excerpt: China's imports of manufactured goods from the United States—excluding cars and planes—there wasn't much change.
result.claim: Excluding cars and planes, Chinese imports of US manufactures fell only as much as China's overall manufactured imports, so the US was not singled out.
result.reason: Targeting is shown only by a decline relative to a comparable baseline.

result.excerpt: I know this goes a bit against the grain
result.claim: The common view holds that China retaliated broadly against US manufactured exports.
result.reason: Conventional narratives should be checked against disaggregated data.

result.excerpt: One theory is that, well, China had already been pretty good at squeezing manufactured imports out of its market
result.claim: The author offers two possible reasons China spared US manufactures, without choosing between them: the remaining imports were essential, or China wanted to keep room for later retaliation.
result.reason: When the cause of a pattern is unclear, competing explanations should be kept open.

result.excerpt: That though is almost all Boeing's fault
result.claim: Cars and planes are exceptions: SUV imports soon rebounded, and the fall in plane imports mostly reflects Boeing's delivery problems rather than Chinese retaliation.
result.reason: Deliveries of capital goods reflect past orders and supplier capacity, not current policy.

result.excerpt: The fall off in energy imports didn't have a big impact on the U.S. economy—there are other markets
result.claim: China did target agriculture and energy; other markets absorbed the lost energy sales, while the agricultural losses had a modest economic but large political impact.
result.reason: Boycotts of fungible commodities are offset by redirected trade, but politically concentrated sectors still feel them.

result.excerpt: I thought U.S. soy would prove to be more of a pure commodity, and the global market would adjust.
result.claim: The author expected US soybeans to find other buyers easily and was surprised by how large China's impact was.
result.reason: Commodity boycotts can bite when the buyer dominates global demand.

result.excerpt: U.S. beans traded at a discount to Brazil (unambiguous evidence of an impact).
result.claim: China's two-thirds share of global soy imports and its total refusal of US beans opened a US discount to Brazilian beans, later partly arbitraged away through routes such as Argentina.
result.reason: A persistent price gap between substitutes shows market segmentation.

result.excerpt: China's revealed capacity to manage its commodity imports over the course of the trade war suggests that it could meet its 2020 agriculture and energy commitments.
result.claim: Because China showed it can steer its commodity imports, and its demand for imported meat is high, it can plausibly meet its 2020 agriculture and energy purchase commitments.
result.reason: A state that can turn off imports at will can also turn them on.

result.excerpt: What China's state gives, China's state can take away.
result.claim: Managed trade makes US farmers hostages: the price of challenging Chinese industrial policy will be renewed retaliation against agriculture, so China is a big but unsafe market.
result.reason: Purchases granted by state direction can be revoked by state direction.

result.claim: The US will eventually have to confront Chinese industrial policy again, since phase one did not address it.
result.reason: Unresolved structural disputes recur in later negotiations.

result.excerpt: it isn't clear the U.S. benefits from exporting say more corn and LNG to China and less to Japan
result.claim: Managed trade may simply divert Chinese imports away from US allies with no net US benefit, though the conventional legal-rules approach also failed to change Chinese policy.
result.reason: Bilateral purchase targets mostly reshuffle trade rather than create it.

result.excerpt: I thought the Economist's article did an admirable job of laying out both the disadvantages
result.claim: The author cites an Economist article for laying out the disadvantages of both managed trade and the conventional approach.
result.reason: Balanced outside analysis helps judge competing policy approaches.
